newsitem.title: HONG KONG: None follow Anglo-US legislature boycott--China.
newsitem.headline: None follow Anglo-US legislature boycott--China.

text.p: British and U.S. ministers were alone in their refusal to attend the inauguration of the new Hong Kong legislature, and their absence would not be missed, a Chinese government spokesman said on Monday.

"Besides the leaders from Britain and the United States, no leaders from other countries have indicated that they would not participate in the inauguration ceremony," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news conference.
"Although they will not participate in the ceremony, it will not affect the whole significance of the event," he added.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, Foreign Minister Robin Cook and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright are boycotting the swearing in of the administration that will run Hong Kong after the territory reverts to China.
Breaking ranks, other main Western allies like Canada and Australia said on Monday they would attend the inauguration.

British and American leaders will attend the midnight (1600 gmt) ceremony at which Britain's Prince Charles will return the colony to China, but they will duck out before the inauguration in the early hours of July 1.
Their absence is meant to protest the investiture of an unelected legislature that will replace Hong Kong's elected council, although officials will be present.
Shen said representatives from other countries indicated that since they came to Hong Kong to see the handover, they should participate in the whole process.
He also noted that even Britain and the United States were sending senior consular diplomats to the inauguration.

London and Washington said earlier this month that they would boycott the swearing-in of the Provisional Legislature, which will sound the death knell of Hong Kong's first fully-elected legislature midway through its four-year term.
But when none of their allies followed their lead, the two hedged their bets by announcing diplomats stationed in the territory would attend the investiture.
China has said the colonial legislature had to go because reformed electoral rules used in the 1995 polls violated previous Sino-British accords.
